data.name: graph_fpt_weights
data.problem: Recover the edge weights of a weighted 3x3 grid graph from empirical first-passage-time distributions r'(t, x, y) of random walks observed only on the boundary vertices (inverse problem for discrete heat equations / random walks on graphs).

notes: Models may only be trained on simulated data; the test split is never used for selection

objectives: Learn a regression model from simulated data (graph_fpt) that solves: Recover the edge weights of a weighted 3x3 grid graph from empirical first-passage-time distributions r'(t, x, y) of random walks observed only on the boundary vertices (inverse problem for discrete h
Select methods by validation rel_l2 only; the test split is used exactly once, at the end
Stay within 900 worker-seconds of compute and 600 s wall time
Eliminate weak approaches with cheap feasibility checks before spending substantial compute
Constraint: Models may only be trained on simulated data; the test split is never used for selection
data.simulator_description: Random walk on a fixed {'family': 'grid', 'rows': 3, 'cols': 3} graph with 9 vertices and 12 edges; edge weights ~ U[0.2, 1.0], mu = degree, potential {'mode': 'none'}. Observed set B = [0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8] (|B|=8). Features: empirical first-passage probabilities r'(t, x, y) for t = 1..9 and (x, y) in B x B from N = 10000 walks per pair, flattened in (t, x, y) order -> 576 features. Target: weights (12 values). Inverse problem: recover graph parameters from boundary first-passage data.

data.title: mean / majority baseline
data.hypothesis: Reference: predicting the training mean. Any useful method must beat it.

author: engineer
summary: exp-0001: mean_baseline at 100% of training data

data.title: Ridge on log first-passage probabilities
data.hypothesis: At t=1, r'(1,x,y) is the transition probability w_xy/mu_x for adjacent boundary pairs. At t=2, paths through the centre give products like (w_x4/mu_x)(w_4y/mu_4). The log transform makes these products additive in log-weights, so the inverse map becomes close to linear. Over the U[0.2,1] range the map from log-weight to weight is smooth enough for a well-regularised linear model to capture most of the variance. The log also stabilises the multiplicative Monte-Carlo noise at small probabilities. This is a strong, cheap baseline for how linear the inverse map really is.

author: ideator-classical
summary: RBF kernel ridge on log features

data.title: RBF kernel ridge on log features
data.hypothesis: The forward map from weights to FPT distributions is smooth and low-dimensional (a 12-dimensional manifold inside 576 dimensions). An RBF kernel interpolant should capture the remaining curvature that linear ridge misses, including the normalisation by mu and the conversion from log-weights back to weights. With n=4000, the O(n^2) kernel is affordable. A small alpha fits the smooth signal while still damping the binomial noise from N=10000 walks per pair.

data.title: PLS on sqrt (variance-stabilised) features
data.hypothesis: Empirical FPT probabilities are binomial proportions, and the sqrt transform roughly equalises their noise variance. The 576 features are highly collinear across t and across symmetric (x,y) pairs. PLS can extract the roughly 12 to 40 latent directions that covary with the weights and discard noise directions, which gives a different bias-variance trade-off from ridge shrinkage.

author: ideator-classical
summary: Quadratic polynomial ridge on PCA-compressed log features

data.title: Quadratic polynomial ridge on PCA-compressed log features
data.hypothesis: The mapping from log-FPT data to weights is near-linear with mild curvature (exp of log-weights, and coupling through the normaliser mu). A second-order Taylor-style expansion in about 60 PCA directions gives about 1.9k features, which is well posed with 4000 samples under ridge. Internal generalised-CV over alpha tunes the regularisation without touching the test split. This explicit low-order nonlinearity sits between linear ridge and an RBF kernel.

summary: Torch MLP on log-FPT features with moderate width and weight decay

data.title: Torch MLP on log-FPT features with moderate width and weight decay
data.hypothesis: The map from edge weights to first-passage probabilities is smooth but multiplicative (products of transition probabilities along paths), so log features make it closer to additive/linear in log-weights. A LayerNorm-GELU MLP with modest weight decay can learn the remaining nonlinearity from 4000 samples, while the small amount of dropout handles Monte Carlo noise from N=10000 walks.

author: ideator-neural
summary: Wide shallow MLP on PCA-compressed sqrt features (noise-whitened)

data.title: Wide shallow MLP on PCA-compressed sqrt features (noise-whitened)
data.hypothesis: The sqrt transform is variance-stabilising for binomial counts (empirical probabilities from N walks), so the noise becomes approximately homoscedastic. PCA to 96 components then removes noise-dominated directions in the 576-dimensional redundant feature space. A wide 2-layer network with higher weight decay should generalise better than a deep one on 4000 samples.

author: ideator-neural
summary: sklearn MLP baseline on log+fpt_summary with L2 regularisation

data.title: sklearn MLP baseline on log+fpt_summary with L2 regularisation
data.hypothesis: This is a cheap, independent neural check that uses a different optimiser stack. Summary statistics such as mean first-passage times and hitting mass are low-noise aggregates that correlate strongly with local conductances, and they complement the per-time log probabilities. Adam with early stopping and alpha=1e-3 tests whether stronger L2 regularisation helps.

data.title: Noise-augmented residual MLP ensemble (custom)
data.hypothesis: Features are Monte Carlo estimates with sampling noise of roughly 1/sqrt(N). Injecting Gaussian input noise during training acts as Tikhonov-like regularisation matched to the measurement noise of the inverse problem. Residual blocks keep optimisation stable at depth. Averaging 3 seeds reduces variance, which matters because the target rel_l2 of 0.05 is tight relative to the noise level.

author: ideator-ensembles
summary: Extra-Trees on log + FPT summary features

data.title: Extra-Trees on log + FPT summary features
data.hypothesis: Edge weights act on first-passage probabilities in a multiplicative way: transition probabilities are w_e/deg-weighted sums, and FPT tails decay geometrically. A log transform makes the map closer to additive, and the FPT summaries (mass, mean time) give compact global signals of local conductances. Extra-Trees fit all 12 outputs jointly, so they share splits across correlated weights. Their randomised thresholds keep variance low against the Monte Carlo noise from N=10000 walks per pair. The model is fast and needs no scaling, which makes it a strong robust nonlinear reference within the budget.

author: ideator-ensembles
summary: Histogram GBM on PCA-rotated log features

data.title: Histogram GBM on PCA-rotated log features
data.hypothesis: The 576 FPT features are highly redundant because many (t,x,y) cells carry the same weight information. Axis-aligned trees struggle when the signal lies along oblique combinations. A PCA rotation to 40 components aligns the informative directions with the axes, cuts per-target boosting cost by about 14x, and denoises the Monte Carlo sampling noise. Boosting then refines the remaining nonlinearity per edge weight, using shallow trees and L2 regularisation to avoid fitting noise.

author: ideator-ensembles
summary: Random Forest on PCA-30 sqrt features (rotation-forest style)

data.title: Random Forest on PCA-30 sqrt features (rotation-forest style)
data.hypothesis: The sqrt transform is variance-stabilising for binomial empirical probabilities (Var ~ p(1-p)/N), so Monte Carlo noise becomes roughly homoscedastic across cells. Thirty principal components keep the dominant smooth modes of the boundary response. A bagged forest with moderate min_samples_leaf on these de-noised oblique axes tests whether variance reduction alone, rather than boosting, is enough for a robust nonlinear fit. It is also diverse from the log/Extra-Trees and GBM runs in transform, rotation and ensembling style.

author: ideator-ensembles
summary: Ridge backbone + per-target histogram boosting on residuals (with ridge preds as features)

data.title: Ridge backbone + per-target histogram boosting on residuals (with ridge preds as features)
data.hypothesis: Around the weight prior the inverse map from FPT data to weights is likely close to linear, but trees are poor at extrapolating smooth linear trends, which limits pure ensembles near rel_l2 0.05. This model first fits a ridge on all log features to capture the global linear inverse. Gradient boosting then fits only the nonlinear residual, using both the features and the 12 ridge estimates. The ridge estimates give trees a near-sufficient low-dimensional summary of the weight vector to split on. The library cannot express this hybrid, which usually beats either component alone on smooth inverse problems.

config.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor

class RidgeResidualGBM(BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin):
    def __init__(self, alpha=1.0, lr=0.08, max_iter=250, max_leaf_nodes=15, l2=1.0, seed=0):
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.lr = lr
        self.max_iter = max_iter
        self.max_leaf_nodes = max_leaf_nodes
        self.l2 = l2
        self.seed = seed

    def _aug(self, X, P):
        return np.hstack([P, X])

    def fit(self, X, y):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float64)
        y = np.asarray(y, dtype=np.float64)
        self._1d = (y.ndim == 1)
        Y = y.reshape(-1, 1) if self._1d else y
        self.ridge_ = Ridge(alpha=self.alpha).fit(X, Y)
        P = self.ridge_.predict(X).reshape(len(X), -1)
        R = Y - P
        Z = self._aug(X, P)
        self.gbms_ = []
        for j in range(Y.shape[1]):
            g = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(learning_rate=self.lr, max_iter=int(self.max_iter), max_leaf_nodes=int(self.max_leaf_nodes), l2_regularization=self.l2, early_stopping=False, random_state=self.seed + j)
            g.fit(Z, R[:, j])
            self.gbms_.append(g)
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float64)
        P = self.ridge_.predict(X).reshape(len(X), -1)
        Z = self._aug(X, P)
        corr = np.column_stack([g.predict(Z) for g in self.gbms_])
        out = P + corr
        return out.ravel() if self._1d else out

def build_model(params: dict, task: str, seed: int):
    return RidgeResidualGBM(alpha=float(params.get('alpha', 1.0)), lr=float(params.get('lr', 0.08)), max_iter=int(params.get('max_iter', 250)), max_leaf_nodes=int(params.get('max_leaf_nodes', 15)), l2=float(params.get('l2', 1.0)), seed=int(seed))

author: ideator-domain
summary: Log-linear inverse: ridge on log first-passage probabilities

data.title: Log-linear inverse: ridge on log first-passage probabilities
data.hypothesis: For mu = degree, the one-step transition is p(x,y) = w_xy / sum_z w_xz. Short-time first-passage probabilities are products and sums of such ratios. Taking logs turns these multiplicative ratio structures into approximately linear relations in log w, so a well-regularised linear map on log features should capture most of the inverse. This gives a cheap, strong, physics-motivated baseline, and the result shows how linear the problem is.

data.title: Variance-stabilised (sqrt/Anscombe) features + torch MLP
data.hypothesis: Each r'(t,x,y) is an empirical multinomial frequency from N=10000 walks, so its noise variance scales with p(1-p). A square-root transform approximately equalises the noise across features, so tiny late-time probabilities are not underweighted and large early ones do not dominate. A LayerNorm MLP can then learn the smooth nonlinear map from heat-kernel-like boundary data to the 12 weights, including combinations involving the hidden centre vertex.

author: ideator-domain
summary: Early-time FPT window + RBF kernel ridge

data.title: Early-time FPT window + RBF kernel ridge
data.hypothesis: Edge weights are most directly identifiable from small t. At t=1, r' is exactly the transition matrix restricted to boundary pairs. At t=2-3, paths through the unobserved centre vertex 4 appear, which pins down the 4 spoke edges. Late-time probabilities are small, noisy and highly collinear. Restricting to the early window removes noise dimensions, and kernel ridge provides a smooth nonlinear interpolant that is well suited to 4000 samples.

author: ideator-domain
summary: Explicit transition-ratio inversion: gauge-fixed log-weight estimates + kernel ridge

data.title: Explicit transition-ratio inversion: gauge-fixed log-weight estimates + kernel ridge
data.hypothesis: The t=1 block gives p(x,y) = w_xy/deg_w(x) for all boundary-to-boundary edges. For an edge-midpoint vertex, the spoke probability to the centre follows from conservation: p(x,4) = 1 - sum of its observed neighbour probabilities. This yields 12 log-ratio equations, log w_xy - mean_z log w_xz = log p(x,y) - mean_z log p(x,z), over the 12 log-weights. The system has rank 11 because transition data is invariant to a global rescaling of w. A pseudo-inverse gives a near-noise-free, gauge-fixed estimate of log w per edge, which is essentially the analytic inverse. A low-dimensional RBF kernel ridge on these physics features (plus the raw log transitions) then only has to learn the residual correction and the prior-driven global scale. Since the scale is not identifiable from the data, the learner should regress it to its conditional mean. This should be far more sample-efficient than learning from 576 raw features.

data.advice:
No idea violates a constraint or is certain to fail, so I'm approving all of them. Points to fix during implementation:

(1) Scale is not identifiable. With mu = weighted degree, the walk depends only on w_e / deg_w, so FPT data cannot determine a global rescaling of the weights. The models can only recover scale from the U[0.2,1.0] prior. Have each run report two numbers: rel_l2 on the weights as given, and rel_l2 after normalising both prediction and target (for example, dividing by their sum). That shows whether the remaining error is mostly the unrecoverable scale, which could make the 0.05 target unreachable for every method.

(2) The log and sqrt transforms need care at zero. With N=10000, many r'(t,x,y) entries at larger t or non-adjacent pairs at t=1 will be exactly 0. Use log(p + c/N) with a fixed constant (for example c=0.5). Fix it in advance rather than tuning it on test. Drop columns that are always zero, such as structurally impossible t=1 pairs, before scaling.

(3) Do all selection on the validation split. This covers PCA dimension, gamma_mult, alpha and epochs. Fit scalers and PCA on train only, then refit on train+val before the single test evaluation.

(4) Budget. Cap the torch MLPs (idea-006, 007, 015) with early stopping on val loss and a wall-clock limit of about 120 s each. For hist_gbm (idea-011, 013), set max_iter with early stopping, since you need 12 per-target models.

(5) Run the cheap, structure-aware ideas first: idea-017 (t=1 ratio inversion), idea-016, idea-002 and idea-003. They will likely be the strongest. If idea-017 works, its gauge-fixed log-ratio features could be fed into the KRR and MLP variants too.

author: ideator-domain

data.title: Stronger-regularised, smoother RBF kernel ridge on early-time FPT window
data.hypothesis: Idea-016 fits train almost perfectly (0.0016) but reaches only 0.0198 on val, so it is variance-dominated. The likely cause is Monte-Carlo noise in r'(t,x,y) from N=10000 walks. The weight-to-FPT map on a 3x3 grid is smooth and low-dimensional: 12 parameters. Raising alpha 10x to 0.01 and widening the kernel (gamma_mult 0.5 -> 0.25) should damp the fit to sampling noise while keeping enough nonlinearity, cutting val rel_l2 by roughly 10-25%.

author: ideator-domain
summary: RBF kernel ridge on variance-stabilised (sqrt) full FPT window

data.title: RBF kernel ridge on variance-stabilised (sqrt) full FPT window
data.hypothesis: Empirical first-passage probabilities are binomial proportions, so their noise variance grows with p. A sqrt transform roughly equalises the noise across features, which made sqrt the best feature set for both PLS and the MLP. Under the RBF distance, a homoscedastic input lets the later time steps (t>early window) contribute weight information without their larger-p noise dominating. A moderate alpha of 0.003 with gamma_mult 0.3 should beat fpt_early's 0.0198 by using all 576 features with balanced noise.

data.advice: All six ideas fit the objective and constraints: they train only on simulated data, select on val, and are affordable on CPU. Kernel ridge on fpt_early (idea-016, val 0.0198) already meets the <=0.05 target. Further work should improve robustness rather than chase small gains. (1) Treat idea-022 and idea-023 as the main candidates. Their alpha/gamma changes directly address the train/val gap, and you should report both train and val rel_l2 so the variance diagnosis can be checked. (2) idea-018 says it uses a 'variance-stabilised early window', but its config uses features=fpt_early, not sqrt. Either fix the config or describe it accurately. 50 PLS components on standardized features may also be close to plain least squares, so add a quick n_components sweep (e.g. 20/35/50) on val. (3) For the MLPs (idea-020, idea-021), use val-based early stopping and cap epochs to stay within the 900 worker-second budget. Report wall time. Do not tune on test. (4) Next round, consider averaging the best kernel-ridge and MLP val predictions in a simple ensemble, and a sqrt-transformed early-time window for kernel ridge. Choose the final model on val only, then evaluate test exactly once.

data.title: PCA-denoised sqrt features + RBF kernel ridge
data.hypothesis: The 576 sqrt features are highly redundant: 12 weights drive a smooth low-dimensional manifold, and sampling noise is spread across all directions. Projecting to 64 principal components removes noise-dominated directions before the RBF distance is computed. That should improve neighbourhood geometry and reduce the overfitting seen in idea-023.

data.title: Wider-bandwidth kernel ridge on early-time FPT window
data.hypothesis: idea-022 (alpha 0.01, gamma 0.25) beat idea-016 (alpha 0.001, gamma 0.5), so the trend favours smoother kernels. Early-time first-passage probabilities are near-polynomial in the weights (short paths), so the inverse map is smooth. author: ideator-domain
summary: Early-time FPT window with robust scaling for kernel ridge

data.title: Early-time FPT window with robust scaling for kernel ridge
data.hypothesis: Early-time first-passage probabilities for distant boundary pairs are tiny and heavy-tailed: many are zero at t=1–2 and Poisson-noisy. Standard scaling lets a few rare-event features dominate RBF distances. Robust (median/IQR) scaling should balance their contributions and give cleaner kernel similarity.

data.title: Kernel ridge on log + FPT summary features with strong regularisation
data.hypothesis: The log transform linearises the product-of-transition-probabilities structure, since path weights multiply. FPT summaries (means and hitting masses) add global conductance information. The earlier log kernel ridge was screened only at 0.33 fraction with weak regularisation. Combining both feature types with alpha 0.01 and gamma_mult 0.2 targets the overfitting critique and could match or beat the sqrt results.

data.advice: All six ideas fit the objective and constraints. None touch the test split, all train only on simulated data, and kernel ridge with n=4000 fits easily within 900 worker-seconds. Val rel_l2 is already about 0.016, well under the 0.05 target, so the remaining work is about robustness and honest reporting rather than reaching the threshold. Notes: (1) idea-029's rationale says gamma_mult 0.3 but its params use 0.35. Log the value actually used. (2) idea-024, 026 and 027 are close neighbours on the alpha/gamma grid. Interpret their val differences against a noise estimate, such as the spread over CV folds or seeds, instead of treating small gaps as real. (3) Choose hyperparameters on val only, then refit on train+val once before the single test evaluation. (4) For idea-028, the log transform needs a fixed epsilon for zero-probability entries. Choose it from train statistics only. (5) Worth comparing next: a per-target averaged ensemble of the best sqrt and early-window models, and a check against the Monte Carlo noise floor. You can estimate that floor by regenerating features for a few fixed weight vectors with fresh walks and measuring how much the predictions vary. If val error is near that floor, further kernel tuning will give little gain.

author: ideator-domain
summary: Wide-bandwidth, low-alpha kernel ridge on log + FPT summary features

data.title: Wide-bandwidth, low-alpha kernel ridge on log + FPT summary features
data.hypothesis: Narrowing the kernel and raising alpha both regularise, but they trade bias and variance differently. A much wider kernel (gamma_mult 0.09) is already smooth, so it can afford a smaller ridge penalty (alpha 0.004). The forward map from weights to log-FPT is smooth and close to log-linear, so a near-linear wide kernel with weak shrinkage should fit the global structure better than a narrow kernel.

Together these should reduce the effective noise in the kernel distance and the val error.
